title: Oyster Bay and Glen Cove: Colonial Patents and Native Land
summary: English governor Edmund Andros claimed town-wide authority for Oyster Bay in 1677 while acknowledging Native land within its boundaries that had not yet been purchased. Separate agreements and resource rights show why this region cannot be explained as one completed sale.

why_this_matters: The patent itself acknowledged Native land that had not been purchased. Naming the English government and settlers behind the claim makes visible how colonial authority could spread beyond particular agreements, without treating a map outline as proof of Native consent or disappearance.
introduction_title: A colonial patent did not prove Native consent
introduction_content: English governor Edmund Andros claimed town-wide authority for Oyster Bay in 1677 while acknowledging Native land within its boundaries that had not yet been purchased. Separate agreements and resource rights show why this region cannot be explained as one completed sale.
history_title: Meadow agreements, English authority and unpurchased Native land
history_content:
A small agreement did not transfer a whole region

Oyster Bay is both a harbor on Long Island Sound and the name of a much larger modern town extending toward the South Shore. Glen Cove is now a separate city on Hempstead Harbor. The earlier 1653 Oyster Bay agreement is interpreted in its own map chapter. This wider regional chapter concerns a different question: how did an English colonial government claim authority across an inhabited Native landscape containing separate agreements and continuing Native interests? The 1677 patent itself answers part of that question by acknowledging land within its boundaries that had not yet been purchased from Native people. Oyster Bay Town Records, Volume I, printed pp. 307–308

A meadow agreement extended settlers' access

The agreement dated March 17, 1658 names Tackapoosha, sachem of Massapeague, and Chopeyconnaws, described as his brother and a young sachem. It names Anthony Wright, Peter Wright, Nicholas Wright, Daniel Whitehead, John Richbill and Samuel Andrews among the Oyster Bay inhabitants receiving the grant. The meadowlands were described through Native place names, including Warrasketuck and Arrasquongue. The printed record lists goods to be delivered by July 1: kettles, guns, clothing, powder, shot and other items, including alcohol. The record does not by itself establish the circumstances in which those terms were negotiated. Oyster Bay Town Records, Volume I, printed pp. 347–348

The grant also allowed the Oyster Bay inhabitants to stack hay and feed cattle on adjoining uplands, and to pass with horses and carts. Those were privileges granted to the settlers, not a reservation of Native cattle rights. The distinction matters: use of resources and access through adjoining land could extend beyond the meadow parcel itself. Reading the terms is more informative than treating a deed as a simple exchange of one bounded piece of property. Oyster Bay Town Records, Volume I, printed pp. 348

Tackapousha names the Matinecock boundary, 1667

Native leaders also testified about where Matinecock land ended. At Killingworth on March 22, 1667, Tackapousha, Sachem of Massapequa, declared that "hemsted men lyes" when they said Matinecock land reached no farther west than Musketa Cove. He had always owned the cove to be Matinecock land; his own land ended at the creek at the head of Hempstead Harbor, and all east of it to Oyster Bay's bounds was Matinecock. He said he could prove it "by many more Indians then hear have testified," and Pamelaci and Nimhai added their marks. Oyster Bay Town Records, volume I, Appendix p. 677

Governor Andros imposed an English legal framework

On September 29, 1677, Edmund Andros, governor under James, Duke of York and Albany, issued the Oyster Bay patent. The named English patentees were Henry Townsend Sr., Nicholas Wright, Thomas Townsend, Gideon Wright, Richard Harcker, Joseph Carpenter and Josias Lating, acting for themselves and the town's freeholders and inhabitants. It described a region bounded through Cold Spring, the Sound, the South Sea, Hempstead Harbor, Cantiagge and other landmarks. Its claim included woods, meadows, waters, fishing, hunting and other resources. Oyster Bay Town Records, Volume I, printed pp. 307–308

The patent placed the grant within an English form of landholding called free and common socage, tied to the manor of East Greenwich in Kent. It required an annual quit-rent of one fat lamb, due March 25, to the Duke's representative. This was not a Native agreement: an English official was assigning land, inheritance and governmental authority through the institutions of an overseas monarchy. Oyster Bay Town Records, Volume I, printed pp. 308

The patent admitted that Native land remained unpurchased

Andros protected other lawful patents and property claims within the stated bounds, while bringing the lands and plantations into the town's government. Crucially, he also said that Native land not already purchased could be purchased later according to colonial law. The patent therefore cannot be read as evidence that every Native owner had already agreed to a transfer, or that every place inside its outline changed hands in 1677. It combined a colonial jurisdictional claim with the prospect of further acquisition. Oyster Bay Town Records, Volume I, printed pp. 308

That distinction changes how this map should be read. A shaded region records the reach of claims and institutions, not a single moment when Native people or relationships ended. The smaller Oyster Bay agreement chapter and the individual place-name entries preserve more specific locations and records. Continue through Matinecock and Massapequa ancestral-land histories to learn about the people connected with this wider region.

Reading the bay islands and barrier beach

The 1677 patent reached toward the South Sea and included waters, meadows and resource rights. Its regional claim therefore matters to the coastal landscape as well as the town’s northern settlement. But the 1658 meadow agreement and its access privileges must not be stretched into an undocumented sale of the entire modern barrier. The patent’s own reference to Native land still unpurchased prevents that reading. The coastal shading uses today’s geography to locate this history, not to draw a single seventeenth-century conveyance. Oyster Bay Town Records, volume I, pp. 307–308 and 347–348
whereintheworld_content: This outline uses modern Oyster Bay and Glen Cove land, including Oyster Bay’s bay islands and portion of the southern barrier, to orient readers from Long Island Sound to the Atlantic shore. It is not the surveyed footprint of the 1653 agreement,1658 meadow grant or 1677 patent. Modern municipal lines divide the barrier; inlets, shores and engineered land have changed. A shaded beach is not proof that every Native right was transferred in one agreement. The patent expressly contemplated Native land not yet purchased. The outline does not establish current ownership or public access. NYS Civil Boundaries: modern orientation
